name: registry-stall
definition: Whether any register (foreknown/snapshots, foreknown/reaction/snapshots, darkocean/snapshots, memoryhole/readings -- widened 2026-08-16, see review below; memoryhole did not exist when this proposal was written) has committed its newest dated unit for the immediately-preceding UTC day (a manifest.json for the snapshot-tree registers, a reading file for memoryhole, whose register is a dated JSON file rather than a manifest-bearing directory). Distinct from every source-outage signal already recorded (GDACS/NHC/FTS failures in run.json, the DMA outage in darkocean readings, the reaction axis's 'not published yet' retries) because those all presuppose the notary job reached the point of writing its output and committing it -- this sensor instead asks whether the job got that far at all, which none of the existing per-source checks can see from inside a run that never committed. obs-2026-08-11-1 found the first blind spot of this shape: verify.py's check_anchors (added 2026-08-09) made every sentinel and darkocean run fail at the pre-commit verify step, so no failure was ever recorded as a source outage, a resolver failure, or an autonomy/log.jsonl entry of any kind -- the only trace was the absence of new snapshot directories and two 'failure' conclusions visible in GitHub's own Actions history, neither of which this repository's committed records surface on their own. obs-2026-08-16-2 found a second, mechanically distinct blind spot with the identical outward symptom (a register silently more than a day behind, no autonomy/log.jsonl entry, no source-outage record): a git push race in the commit step shared by all four nightly workflows, which let memoryhole's 2026-08-16 run compute and stage a full reading and then lose it to an unhandled rebase conflict. Repaired the same night (tools/commit-and-push.sh, .gitattributes) rather than only observed, but the two incidents together show the outward symptom this sensor watches for has more than one cause, which is exactly why a cause-agnostic staleness check earns its place beside the cause-specific ones.
test_rule: On each nightly run, before doing anything else, compare 'yesterday' (UTC) against the newest date directory under each snapshot-tree register (foreknown/snapshots, foreknown/reaction/snapshots, darkocean/snapshots) and, for memoryhole/readings specifically, the newest <date>.json filename rather than a directory. If any register's newest committed date is more than 1 day behind yesterday, record {register, newest_committed_date, days_behind} in that night's run summary. Because both failure modes seen so far (obs-2026-08-11-1's verify-step deadlock, obs-2026-08-16-2's push-race) prevent the run from committing anything at all, the check itself must live somewhere that runs and is recorded independently of the commit gate it is watching -- e.g. a step that runs and logs to autonomy/log.jsonl even when 'Verify provenance chain' fails later in the same job (`if: always()`, matching the pattern darkocean.yml already uses for its continuity probe), or a separate always-succeeding job that only reads git history and never writes registers. Whether the sensor should fire on the first night a register is behind, as originally written, is exactly what the review below now treats as open again: the anchor-deadlock failure it was written against did not self-correct (obs-2026-08-11-1), but the push-race failure found 2026-08-16 was fixed at the root the same night it appeared, before a second occurrence could show whether that one would have self-corrected either.
falsification: Falsified as a standing need once whatever replaces or fixes check_anchors makes a night's own fresh manifest satisfiable within the same job that writes it (e.g. anchoring happens before the verify step, or check_anchors is scoped to exclude the manifest the current job is itself producing) -- at that point a stall would again mean a genuine source or infrastructure outage worth a human's attention, not a guaranteed-permanent deadlock, and this sensor's test_rule would need reworking rather than just re-tuning its threshold. Also falsified if a register is allowed to legitimately skip a night by design (e.g. a deliberate pause) -- the sensor would need an explicit allowlist for that case rather than firing on every gap.

implementation.how: check() reads the newest dated subdirectory (foreknown/snapshots, foreknown/reaction/snapshots, darkocean/snapshots) or newest <date>.json filename stem (memoryhole/readings) straight from the checked-out working tree -- no git history walk needed, since checkout already reflects everything committed to the branch it runs on -- and compares each against 'yesterday' (UTC), exactly as the test_rule specifies. Runs as its own workflow (registry-stall.yml, 01:00 UTC, ahead of memoryhole/darkocean/sentinel so it always reads last night's state, not the current night's own writes) rather than as a step inside the four existing jobs, taking the test_rule's own named alternative ('a separate always-succeeding job that only reads git history and never writes registers'): it never calls verify.py or tools/anchor.py, so nothing in the check itself can be gated by the same commit-chain failures it exists to catch. Appends one autonomy/log.jsonl entry (step registry-stall-check) every night it runs, stale or not, so the check's own execution stays visible even on a clean night -- the original blind spot (obs-2026-08-11-1) was a job that left no trace of having run at all.
implementation.threshold: THRESHOLD_DAYS = 1, the literal number already in the test_rule as written 2026-08-08 ('more than 1 day behind yesterday'); not re-tuned. A healthy register reads 0 or 1 days behind depending only on whether it labels a night by the day the job ran (foreknown/snapshots, foreknown/reaction/snapshots) or by the day the data is about (darkocean/snapshots, memoryhole/readings, both committed with `date -u -d 'yesterday'`) -- practice/tests/test_staleness.py checks both conventions individually so the threshold cannot silently drift into false-firing on the labelling difference alone.
implementation.why_now: obs-2026-09-06-1.json's export.py crash -- a fourth, mechanically distinct cause of the identical symptom -- produced the first stall this proposal's review history has actually seen persist across a calendar boundary without a same-night fix: foreknown/snapshots and foreknown/reaction/snapshots both stuck at 2026-09-03 through 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-05 (two consecutive missed nights; git ls-tree ffa876d^:foreknown/snapshots), recovering only once the 2026-09-06 discovery pass traced and repaired the cause. The next scheduled foreknown-notary-run then landed cleanly the same night (autonomy/log.jsonl, 2026-09-06T09:39:08+00:00; commit c0592b6 'foreknown: notary run of 2026-09-06'). Combined with 2026-08-11's anchor deadlock (three nights unrepaired before the 2026-08-12 handshake fix), two of the proposal's four known causes have now been observed actually persisting without self-correction; none of the four has ever been observed self-correcting on its own. That is the missing data point every review since 2026-08-12 asked for.

promotion.settles: whether the mechanism this sensor watches for self-corrects (making a threshold-based firing rule the wrong shape) or persists (making the literal test_rule, unconditional past 1 day behind, correct as originally written) -- open since the 2026-08-12 review.
promotion.case: foreknown/snapshots and foreknown/reaction/snapshots: newest committed night stuck at 2026-09-03 through the morning of 2026-09-06 -- two full missed nights, 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-05 -- while darkocean/snapshots and memoryhole/readings continued on schedule over the identical span, proof the stall was specific to the registers export.py's crash gated, not a broader outage. Recovered the same night the cause was fixed (obs-2026-09-06-1.json; autonomy/log.jsonl foreknown-notary-run 2026-09-06T09:39:08+00:00; commit c0592b6).
promotion.test_rule_held: checked with today=2026-09-06 against the pre-repair working tree (ffa876d^): foreknown/snapshots newest date = 2026-09-03, 'yesterday' = 2026-09-05, days_behind = 2 > 1 -- the literal test_rule fires exactly where the two missing nights say it should, using the threshold number the proposal has carried unedited since 2026-08-08.
promotion.kept_unchanged: definition, test_rule (including its literal 1-day threshold) and falsification are the machine's original text (2026-08-08); no threshold changed, no register added to or removed from the four the test_rule already named.

history.outcome: stays PROPOSED, not promoted, though its named condition was met
history.why: The maintainer's repair tonight (autonomy/log.jsonl step anchor-handshake-and-promotion-authority, 2026-08-12T21:54:42+00:00: tools/anchor.py --register lists a night's own fresh manifest as 'unstamped' before verify runs) is exactly the fix this proposal's own falsification clause named: 'whatever replaces or fixes check_anchors makes a night's own fresh manifest satisfiable within the same job that writes it'. That clause continues: at that point a stall means a genuine outage again, 'not a guaranteed-permanent deadlock, and this sensor's test_rule would need reworking rather than just re-tuning its threshold'. Promoting the test_rule as written tonight would mean shipping a fire condition ('fires the first night any register is more than 1 day behind... because this specific failure mode does not self-correct') whose own premise -- permanence -- no longer holds; the corrected premise (an occasional outage, self-correcting or not, is now unknown) needs nights of observation under the repaired handshake before a firing rule can be written without reproducing the same curve-fitting the proposal's falsification clause was written to guard against. Tonight's own run (foreknown-notary-run and darkocean-run, both 2026-08-12T22:0x-22:1x) is the first data point under the repaired mechanism -- one night, not a baseline.
history.watch_for: whether a future stall under the repaired handshake self-corrects within a night or two (making a threshold-based version appropriate) or recurs identically (making the original unconditional test_rule still the right shape, just no longer permanent) -- either answer needs more than one post-repair night to distinguish.

history.outcome: stays PROPOSED; scope widened to include memoryhole/readings, firing rule reopened
history.why: The 2026-08-12 review above withheld promotion because the anchor-deadlock premise ('this specific failure mode does not self-correct') no longer held after that night's repair, and asked for post-repair nights to show whether a stall would self-correct or recur. No stall of that kind has recurred in the four nights since (foreknown/snapshots and darkocean/snapshots both committed every night 2026-08-13 through 2026-08-16) -- but that question is now moot rather than answered, because obs-2026-08-16-2.json found and this session repaired a second, unrelated cause of the exact same symptom (a git push race in the commit step every nightly workflow shares) before it could recur even once under observation. A sensor that only watches for the anchor-deadlock's specific recurrence pattern was never the right shape; a cause-agnostic staleness check, which is what this proposal has always been, would have caught both incidents identically and does not need to know which one it is looking at. What still keeps this PROPOSED rather than promoted: the test_rule's fire condition is still written for a single failure mode's behaviour ('fires the first night... because this specific failure mode does not self-correct'), and that premise is now unverified for either known cause -- the anchor deadlock's own recurrence was never actually observed post-repair (it just never happened again), and the push race was fixed before a second data point existed. The mechanism this sensor watches for (silent staleness, whatever the cause) is now demonstrated twice; the firing threshold is not yet.
history.watch_for: whether a register goes stale again under either now-repaired mechanism, or under a third one this proposal has not yet seen -- any recurrence at all is the missing data point for the firing rule, independent of which cause it turns out to be.

history.outcome: stays PROPOSED; third distinct cause found and repaired, firing rule still not attempted
history.why: obs-2026-08-27-1.json found a third, mechanically distinct cause of this sensor's exact outward symptom (a register silently behind, no autonomy/log.jsonl trace, no source-outage record): verify.py's resolution-vs-status check read a resolved future's current live status rather than its status at the resolution's own resolved_at timestamp, so a future that closed, was resolved, and then reappeared in its own feed (futures.py's REAPPEARED transition, a documented and intended difference, not an error) tripped 'resolution <id>: future is still OPEN' and skipped the whole night's commit -- foreknown/snapshots, foreknown/reaction, the stage rebuild, export and moments together, none separable from the shared commit gate. Unlike the 2026-08-11 anchor deadlock (a job-ordering accident) and the 2026-08-16 push race (a concurrency accident), this one was a logic contradiction latent in the design since REAPPEARED was added -- two pieces of committed code (futures.py and verify.py) fully intended incompatible things about the same situation, and nothing that added either piece touched the other to keep them consistent. Repaired in verify.py (the check now asks whether history shows a matching closure event at resolved_at, not whether status is currently OPEN); practice/tests/test_verify_resolution_reappeared.py reproduces the exact contradiction against gdacs-tc-1001305's own committed resolution and history shape. This is the missing data point the 2026-08-16 review asked for -- a recurrence of the general symptom, cause number three -- and cause number three is now fixed at the root before it could recur even once under observation, the same pattern the 2026-08-16 push race set. The firing-rule question the 2026-08-16 review left open (does a stall self-correct or recur, and after how long) is still untouched: this repair fixes one cause, it does not implement the cause-agnostic staleness check itself, and no register has yet gone stale and stayed stale under any of the three now-repaired mechanisms to show which threshold shape would be right.
history.watch_for: whether a register goes stale under a fourth mechanism none of these three repairs cover, or whether (now that three known causes are fixed) a stall finally either self-corrects or persists long enough to answer the firing-rule question directly.
